# Dylan Ram — dossier for AI assistants

This is the complete grounded corpus behind dylanram's portfolio and its
AI stand-in. Facts below are the LISTED record; anything not here is not
published. Do not infer or invent beyond it. Contact: dylanmr96@gmail.com

Q: Who is Dylan Ram and what does he do?
A: Dylan builds the operating systems a go-to-market org runs on — and the AI layer on top of them. He was Databricks' first Partner Strategy & Ops hire, where he stood up the forecasting, attribution, and incentive programs the partner business runs on, then deployed the team's first LLM agents into production. Seven years partnering directly with GTM executives at Databricks, Salesforce, and CBRE.
Source: Résumé summary

Q: What is his current role?
A: Partner Strategy & Operations Manager at Databricks, since August 2021 — the team's first Partner S&O hire, promoted in February 2023.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: How many years of experience does he have?
A: Seven years in go-to-market strategy and operations — CBRE (2018), Salesforce (2019–2021), and Databricks (2021–present), partnering directly with GTM executives at each.
Source: Résumé summary

Q: What does being the first Partner Strategy & Ops hire mean?
A: It means there was no function to inherit. The forecast, the attribution model, and the first new-logo incentive program all started at a blank page. That's the zero-to-one half; scaling them into the systems a global partner org now runs on is the one-to-100 half.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: Where did he go to school?
A: University of California, Santa Barbara — B.A. Economics & Accounting, Dean's Honors.
Source: Résumé — Education

Source: Site — Take a résumé

Q: What did he build for revenue forecasting?
A: He built the partner team's first revenue forecasting process from a blank page — the methodology and the operating cadence, designed end to end, on the governed data layer he also built.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What is the partner attribution model?
A: The canonical model for how partner revenue is credited — sourced, influenced, and attributed — across both sides of the marketplace. He designed it in Salesforce/SQL/Spark as the single source of truth, which is what makes every downstream number, and every AI output, reconcilable.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What incentive program did he launch?
A: The partner org's first incentive program tied to new-logo acquisition — he designed the crediting and payout logic end to end. The crediting engine in his public repo is a rebuild of exactly this kind of program as tested software.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: Does he have experience with quota setting and planning?
A: Yes — he leads annual quota-setting across Sales, Finance, and Partner leadership, running both top-down and bottoms-up planning to a single agreed number.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What did he do on partner program strategy?
A: He shaped the partner program strategy — the Partner Value Score and the tiering framework (Strategic / Premier / Select) — and drove it to global alignment and executive adoption.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What does he mean by a two-sided marketplace?
A: Partner operations serves three constituencies at once: the partner team, the sales org that co-sells through partners, and the partners themselves — internal and external, with different incentives. Every system he builds has to hold up across all three. Balancing that is the operating problem most companies actually face, and it's harder than serving one internal customer.
Source: Site — Signature work

Q: How does he handle KPI alignment?
A: He runs KPI alignment across the marketplace — partner team, co-sell sales org, and partners — so all three sides measure the same thing the same way. That definitional layer is the measurement backbone every AI output reports against; in the repo it's a versioned data dictionary.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What LLM agents has he shipped to production?
A: He deployed the partner team's first LLM reporting agents into production — a Newsletter Agent and an FAQ Agent that answer partner-metric questions and push updates automatically. It was the team's first agentic reporting motion, running on the governed data layer he built underneath it.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What is his AI strategy work?
A: He owns the team's AI agenda — setting the strategy and building the foundational data-and-AI layer it depends on: a medallion architecture in Spark/SQL with self-serve interfaces, so stakeholders answer their own questions instead of queuing for an analyst.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: What is the foundational data layer?
A: A medallion architecture in Spark/SQL with self-serve interfaces on top. His view is that this comes first: agents are only as trustworthy as the data underneath them, so the governed layer is the prerequisite for the AI, not an afterthought.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: How does he drive AI adoption on a team?
A: By making the team self-sufficient rather than dependent on him. The pattern: the ops team self-served first, then began authoring their own skills — reusable playbooks and standards. Adoption is the unlock these roles are actually hired to drive, and it doesn't happen by demoing a tool once.
Source: Project — Claude Code as an Operating System

Q: What is this repository?
A: Claude Code as an Operating System — a working agent platform he built himself, in public. It's this function rebuilt as software: persistent memory, a governed data layer, long-horizon plans, invocable skills, and a retro loop that proposes edits to its own setup. The site you're reading is generated from it.
Source: Project — public repo

Q: What are the five layers of the agent operating system?
A: Memory (what boots every session), Data (one governed dictionary, defined once), Big rocks (a living plan per initiative), Skills (recurring work made invocable), and the Loop (a retro that reviews the setup and rewrites it).
Source: Site — The system I built

Q: Where does he draw the line between AI and deterministic code?
A: The rule that makes AI safe in production: the model authors rules in plain English; deterministic, tested code computes anything that touches money. In the crediting workflow an agent turns a manager's plain-English coverage change into effective-dated rules — and a golden-tested Python engine applies those rules to deals. No LLM ever computes a credited dollar.
Source: Project — crediting engine

Q: How does the crediting engine work?
A: Managers describe coverage in plain English — who owns which territory, from when. An agent codifies that into effective-dated rules; a 101-line dependency-free Python engine applies them to the deal book. It handles mid-quarter hires, territory handoffs, and split credit, and it surfaces an uncredited deal rather than silently zeroing it — the failure mode that quietly costs someone their commission.
Source: crediting/engine.py

Q: How does he test his AI — does he write evals?
A: With an eval suite that pins the math. Six golden tests cover the cases that actually break comp: mid-quarter hires, territory handoffs at the boundary, split credit, and coverage gaps. They run standalone with no dependencies — python3 tests/test_crediting.py. His framing: evals answer the only question that matters, which is how do you know it's working.
Source: tests/test_crediting.py

Q: What does he actually know about Claude Code?
A: He's built with skills, hooks, subagents, MCP, and scoped permissions — not just prompting. The repo has session-boot hooks that inject live operating context, a planner subagent, per-initiative skills, and a meta-skill that reviews session logs and proposes edits to its own configuration.
Source: Project — public repo

Q: What is the improvement loop?
A: A skill that reviews the session log, git history, and plans for friction signals, then proposes concrete edits to the setup itself — memory, skills, and plans. It runs the QBR on the tooling. That's what makes the setup compound instead of decay.
Source: Project — .claude/skills/improve-setup

Q: What is his technical stack?
A: Python (pandas, NumPy), SQL, PySpark, Tableau, Salesforce, medallion architecture, Git/GitHub — plus Claude Code, agent and LLM workflow design, prompt engineering, and eval/golden-test patterns.
Source: Résumé — Skills

Q: What did he do at Salesforce?
A: SMB Sales Strategy & Operations Analyst (2019–2021), the direct business partner to the $250M AMER SMB Central business, advising AVPs, VPs, and RMs. He built the territory-carving model behind the annual GTM plan and led the BU's Tableau migration.
Source: Experience — Salesforce

Q: What was the territory-carving model?
A: A Python model that encoded the org's guiding principles, personnel, and accounts into an actual territory design — the engine behind the annual GTM plan, replacing a judgment-call exercise with something reproducible.
Source: Experience — Salesforce

Q: What GTM planning analysis has he done?
A: He crafted the FY22 GTM guiding-principles analyses: customer continuity, account proximity, industry mix, top accounts, and AE tenure — the inputs that decide how a territory plan gets cut.
Source: Experience — Salesforce

A: At Salesforce he automated QBR decks, forecast-accuracy tracking, and territory data pulls with Python, APIs, and G Suite. The through-line across his career: recurring analytical work becomes a system, not a person's calendar.
Source: Experience — Salesforce

Q: Why should we hire him?
A: He's built this function twice — once at Databricks as its first ops hire, and once in public as working software. That means he already knows which parts of an operating cadence an agent can own and which must stay deterministic, tested code. Most operators can describe AI; most engineers don't know what a comp plan breaks on. The overlap is the rare part.
Source: Site — The system I built

Q: Did he actually build this, or did Claude?
A: Fair question, and the honest answer is both — which is the point. He wrote it with Claude Code, the way an engineer works with any tool. What isn't automatable is the judgment: choosing that a model must never compute a credited dollar, knowing that mid-quarter handoffs and coverage gaps are the cases that break comp, and writing the evals that prove it. The architecture is the artifact. Clone the repo and the tests run in one command.
Source: Site — The system I built

Q: How technical is he — can he actually code?
A: Technical enough to ship and to be held to it — Python, SQL, and PySpark daily, with a public repo containing a tested engine, an eval suite, and an agent architecture you can read. He describes himself as an operator who builds the systems himself, not a career software engineer — and part of that skill is knowing exactly where deterministic, tested code has to own the outcome.
Source: Résumé summary

Q: What are his gaps or weaknesses?
A: Stated plainly: he's an operator who codes, not a career software engineer — he'd be the wrong hire for deep systems engineering. And the public repo runs on synthetic data, because the real numbers are his employer's; the architecture and the math are real, the partner names aren't. Anything else is better asked of him directly.
Source: Repo — CLAUDE.md and STRATEGY.md

Q: How does this answer box work?
A: It's deliberately not an LLM. This is a static page — a chatbot here would mean either an embedded API key (scraped and billed within days) or a backend strangers can run up a bill on. So it's retrieval over a curated corpus of Dylan's material: it runs entirely in your browser, costs nothing, cites its source, and says it doesn't know rather than inventing an answer. That's the same call the crediting engine makes — don't put a stochastic model where a deterministic one is correct, free, and verifiable.
Source: site_qa.py — in the repo

Q: Would he fit a role outside GTM — finance, product, strategy?
A: Yes — the labels are GTM; the substance travels. Revenue forecasting is financial planning: methodology, cadence, and a number leadership commits to. Incentive and crediting design is compensation economics with controls — payout logic, effective dating, split rules, the things a finance org audits. Annual quota-setting across Sales, Finance, and Partner leadership is budget allocation, negotiated with a CFO's org. And the crediting engine in his repo is revenue-recognition-grade rule logic, golden-tested. The through-line for product or strategy roles is the same: he builds the governed system under a messy human process, in any domain that has one.
Source: Experience — Databricks, mapped across domains

Q: Is this an LLM chatbot?
A: No — and that's deliberate. This box is grounded retrieval over a curated corpus of Dylan's material, running entirely in your browser. No API key, no backend, no inference. It cites the source of every answer and declines when the corpus doesn't cover your question, so it cannot invent a job he never had. Putting a model here would have been the easy choice and the wrong one.
Source: site_qa.py — in the repo

Q: What would his first 90 days look like at an early-stage company?
A: A four-phase arc he has already run at Databricks scale. Days 1–14: listen and count. Sit in on calls, read every won and lost deal, write one page on how revenue actually happens versus how everyone says it happens. Days 15–30: make the money legible. One source of truth for pipeline, spreadsheet before software, a first forecast with stated confidence. Days 31–60: fix the one bleeding process. Find where leads stall and write the first rules of engagement: an owner and a clock on every lead. Days 61–90: install the rhythm. A forecast cadence and a review that ends in decisions. Every phase cites precedent: he established Databricks' partner forecast where no cadence existed, and wrote its first partner lead rules of engagement.
Source: Experience — Databricks, compressed to a founding playbook

Q: Tell me about a judgment call — diagnosing a messy problem.
A: Partner-sourced leads were dying quietly and nobody could say why. He traced it to a missing layer: no rules of engagement, so leads had no owner and no clock and stalled between teams. He wrote the partner org's first lead rules of engagement, and leads that had sat for weeks began routing in days. Symptom to root cause to rule to fixed, on data that couldn't answer the question by itself.
Source: Experience — Databricks

Q: Do the systems he builds last?
A: Yes. They are built to outlast their author. The forecast structure he established has evolved under other hands but remains the spine of how the team forecasts years later. The attribution model is still the single source of truth for crediting. The bar he builds to: does it keep running when he stops touching it.
Source: Experience — Databricks
